title: Half of last week's 3,339 paper trades won. The desk still lost $59,853.
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Saw the options bot thread here this week leading with how often it wins, and it made me pull the other half of that sentence for my own desk.

This is the house paper desk I run, Oct 12-16. 3,339 trades closed and 1,669 of them won. About a coin flip, which sounds fine until you split it:

- Stocks: 2,956 closed, average winner $19, average loser $19, week +$1,435.
- Options: 383 closed, 146 won, average winner $252, average loser $414, week -$61,287.

So the stocks did basically nothing and 383 option bets did all the damage. Fewer than 4 in 10 of them won, and the losers ran about 1.6x the size of the winners. Nobody signs up for that bet when it's written down like this, but a bot will happily take it 383 times in a week.

What I haven't settled: cut the options side, cap the size per contract, or leave it alone because one week of options is too small to judge. 14 Friday calls were still open at the bell, so Monday's settle may still move the line.

That split is the reason Quantradin, the tool I made, puts the average loser right next to the average winner. You describe a rule (or paste Pine/Python), it replays it over past prices with options filled at the bid or ask, never the middle, and only the survivors go on to run on paper. Free and paper only, quantradin.com.

Which of these numbers would you have looked at first?

comments.author: ciaranwalsh96
comments.body:
The first number I would inspect is expectancy per unit of risk, not win rate:

p(win) × average win − p(loss) × average loss, calculated after fees and by strategy, underlying and expiry bucket.

Using the headline option averages, the rough closed-trade expectancy is already about -$160 per trade before any additional cost adjustment. But I would not decide from that aggregate alone. A few high-notional contracts or one expiry regime may be driving it, and the 14 open Friday calls create right-censoring: the closed-trade sample may systematically exclude positions that survived longer.

Before cutting the options sleeve, normalize P&L by premium at risk or predefined maximum loss, then report the distribution rather than only the mean: median, 5th percentile, expected shortfall, maximum loss, and contribution by symbol, expiration, days-to-expiry, direction and strategy rule. Also separate entry quality from exit policy by replaying the same signals with fixed exits or capped losses.

For a decision rule, I would pre-register a forward paper window and a risk budget. Stop adding new option risk if cumulative loss, expected shortfall or slippage breaches the threshold; do not keep the sleeve simply to wait for the win rate to “recover.” One week may be too short to estimate an edge, but it is enough to identify whether position sizing or a loss tail can damage the entire desk.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, that's the number the headline hides, and you got there faster than I did. the fleet is every paper bot on Quantradin, which I built, so cutting it by expiry bucket is a query I can run this week. my bet is the short dated stuff carries most of that loss.

comments.author: Comfortable-Chain14
comments.body: Have you made any money yet?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: no. that desk is paper, every one of those 3,339 trades was fake money, which is the whole point of Quantradin, the thing I built: find out which rules break before real cash is on them. quantradin.com
